issues.legal_issue: Retrospective reclassification of non-permanent tenants as permanent tenants, coupled with a limited opportunity to contest that status, cannot constitutionally reduce landholders’ vested right to the purchase price payable for the tenants’ acquisition of the land.
material_facts: Before the challenged amendment, tenants who were not permanent tenants acquired the land on the statutory purchase date, leaving the former landholders entitled to a purchase price determined under the tenancy law.

The amendment deemed tenants meeting specified historical possession conditions to be permanent tenants, changing the applicable purchase-price regime and reducing the amount payable to the former landholders.

The amendment provided that the tenants’ status would be entered in the public record unless the landholder applied to contest it within six months; the Court held that, after that period, the landholder had no effective further opportunity to contest the claim.
The landholders’ right to receive the purchase price had become a property right after the relationship between them and the tenants changed from landlord and tenant to creditor and debtor.
issues.conclusion: Sections 3, 4 and 6 were unconstitutional and void insofar as they deemed certain tenants to be permanent tenants, because their combined effect retrospectively reduced the landholders’ property right and imposed an unreasonable restriction not justified under Article 19(5).
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 19(1)(f), a vested right to receive a debt is property; legislation that retrospectively removes a substantial part of that right must satisfy Article 19(5), and a time-limited procedure that gives the affected holder no real opportunity to contest the deprivation is not a reasonable restriction in the interests of the general public. Applying Bombay Dyeing and Manufacturing Co. Ltd. v. State of Bombay, [1958] SCR 1122, the Court treated the purchase-price entitlement as property. Sri Ram Ram Narain Medhi v. State of Bombay, [1959] Supp. 1 SCR 489, supported the conclusion that the tenants’ title had passed on the statutory purchase date and that the former landholders were thereafter creditors entitled to the purchase price under sections 32 and 32H of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_land_tenure_legislation and (tenants_acquired_title_before_amendment and landholders_retained_purchase_debt) and amendment_retroactively_reclassified_tenants and amendment_reduced_purchase_entitlement and landholders_had_only_limited_time_to_contest_status

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_tenure_: The proceeding challenged the constitutional validity of legislation governing land tenure.
predicates.tenants_acquired_title_before_amendment: Tenants had acquired title to the land under the law before the challenged amendment was enacted.
predicates.landholders_retained_purchase_debt: After title passed, the former landholders retained a right to receive a purchase price from the tenants.
predicates.amendment_retroactively_reclassified_ten: The amendment retrospectively treated some tenants who had not previously been permanent tenants as permanent tenants.
predicates.amendment_reduced_purchase_entitlement: The reclassification changed the applicable purchase-price regime and reduced the amount the former landholders could receive.
predicates.landholders_had_only_limited_time_to_con: The amendment required landholders to contest tenants’ status within a limited period and provided no effective later opportunity to do so.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns an amendment that retrospectively reclassifies tenants, reduces a purchase debt already owed to landholders, and gives them only a limited chance to contest the reclassification, the amendment’s reduction of that vested debt is unconstitutional.

issues.legal_issue: Legislation affecting a purchase debt after the landlord-tenant relationship has ended is not protected as estate reform and is outside legislative competence when its substance does not concern rights in land or the landlord-tenant relationship.
material_facts: By the time the challenged amendment affected the purchase-price entitlement, the tenants’ title had passed and the former landholders and tenants stood in a creditor-debtor relationship.

The challenged provisions affected the former landholders’ entitlement to money rather than acquiring an estate or rights in an estate for the State, or extinguishing or modifying rights in an estate.

The Court found that the provisions’ true effect was to reduce the purchase price through the device of redefining permanent tenancy, rather than to regulate a subsisting landlord-tenant relationship.
issues.conclusion: Article 31A did not protect the challenged provisions, and, in their true effect, they were colourable legislation outside the State Legislature’s competence.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31A does not apply where the challenged law neither provides for State acquisition of an estate or rights in it nor extinguishes or modifies such rights, and where the relevant relationship has already become one of creditor and debtor. Legislative competence is determined by the law’s true scope and effect; under K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa, [1954] SCR 1, legislation is colourable when an apparent exercise of power disguises a substantive transgression of its limits. The Court held that the provisions did not fall within the relevant entries of List II or List III; the dissent considered the legislation supported by Entry 18 of List II, but that was not the Court’s holding.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_tenure_: The proceeding challenged the constitutional validity of legislation governing land tenure.
predicates.creditor_debtor_relationship_had_replace: The tenants had acquired title, leaving the former landholders and tenants in a creditor-debtor relationship.
predicates.challenged_law_changed_money_entitlement: The challenged law altered the former landholders’ entitlement to money owed by the tenants.
predicates.state_did_not_acquire_estate_or_estate_r: The State did not acquire an estate or rights in an estate under the challenged law.
predicates.law_substance_was_not_landlord_tenant_re: The law’s true effect was to alter a debt after the landlord-tenant relationship had ended, rather than to regulate that relationship.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a law that alters a money entitlement after the landlord-tenant relationship has ended, without State acquisition of an estate or estate rights, and whose substance is not landlord-tenant regulation, the law is outside legislative competence and is not protected as estate reform.
